instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A dentist asks: 'Is joint hypermobility relevant to temporomandibular disorders?' Answer based on the article.
input: Several studies have linked temporomandibular joint (TMJ) hypermobility to temporomandibular joint dysfunction (TMD), including in children. Nosouhian et al. characterized 69 patients with TMJ hypermobility and found that a maximal mouth opening (MMO) of <55 or >65 mm was associated with more TMJ discomfort than an intermediate degree of MMO. TMJ hypermobility was more common in women than men, and increased MMO was also correlated with more TMJ sounds and more pain in the masticatory muscles. Westling studied 360 patients with TMD; a subset analysis of 74 females with GJH compared to 73 controls showed a significant association of GJH and TMD. In a national study in Finland involving 6227 participants, TMJ pain was often associated with palpable pain of the neck and shoulder musculature, widespread pain, chronic illness, and female gender. Given that those with hEDS often have most if not all of the additional variables, it would suggest that TMD in this population is complex, common, and must use a more holistic approach to treat.
output:
Yes:
- TMJ hypermobility has been linked to TMD, including in children.
- In 69 patients with TMJ hypermobility, a maximal mouth opening below 55 mm or above 65 mm was associated with more discomfort than intermediate opening. Larger opening correlated with more joint sounds and more masticatory muscle pain. TMJ hypermobility was more common in women.
- In a case-control analysis, generalized hypermobility was significantly associated with TMD.
- TMJ pain in the general population often comes with neck and shoulder muscle pain, widespread pain, chronic illness and female sex, all of which are common in hEDS.

TMD in hEDS is therefore common and multifactorial. Use a holistic approach that also addresses neck and shoulder pain and widespread pain, rather than treating the jaw alone.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A pain clinician asks: 'Is there objective evidence of central sensitization in adults with hEDS?' Answer based on the study.
input: Results: The EDS-HT patient group demonstrated significantly lower PPTs compared to the control group for all zones. The mean (SD) PPT was 2.9 (1.62) kg/cm2 in the EDS-HT patients and 5.2 (1.88) kg/cm2 in the controls (P<0.001). Also at asymptomatic (pain-free) zones, EDS-HT patients systematically showed significantly lower pain thresholds compared to the healthy subjects.
output:
Yes. In 23 women with EDS-HT compared with 23 age- and sex-matched controls, mean pressure pain thresholds were markedly lower (2.9 versus 5.2 kg/cm², P<0.001) across all 14 tested sites. Crucially, they were also lower at sites where patients reported no pain.

Reduced thresholds remote from symptomatic areas indicate generalized secondary hyperalgesia, which is consistent with central sensitization. The study found no confounding factors that explained the differences.

Clinical implication: in many patients, pain cannot be explained solely by local joint pathology. Management should include strategies that target central pain processing alongside joint stabilization.

instruction: You are a health educator answering a patient's question. Based on the study, does joint hypermobility affect men and women differently?
input: Generalized joint hypermobility and hypermobile EDS were significantly higher in females (Table 2). The most common classes are localized asymptomatic joint hypermobility in women and localized hypermobility spectrum disorders in men (Table 1). The prevalence of skin striae was significantly higher in females, while soft tissue problems and Marfanoid habitus was significantly higher among male participants (p<0.05) (Table 3).
output: Yes, the study shows notable differences between sexes. Generalized joint hypermobility and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome were significantly more common in women. When looking at specific types, women most frequently had localized asymptomatic joint hypermobility (flexible joints in a specific spot without pain), whereas men more often experienced localized hypermobility spectrum disorders (localized flexibility accompanied by symptoms or issues). Additionally, women showed a higher rate of skin striae (stretch marks), while men more frequently had soft tissue problems (like tendonitis or bursitis) and features resembling Marfanoid habitus.

instruction: A patient asks: 'Why do I get dizzy, have a racing heart and feel foggy when I stand up? Could this be related to my hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: POTS, NMH, and orthostatic intolerance are common manifestations in hEDS. A study focused on hEDS highlighted POTS as the most prevalent autonomic profile in hEDS and identified sympathetic neurogenic dysfunction as the most likely explanation for dysautonomia in this condition, although connective tissue laxity and vasoactive medication may also play a role. Cardiovascular dysautonomia can easily explain orthostatic intolerance, palpitations, tachycardia, and atypical chest pain, as well as a series of neurological secondary manifestations, including fatigue, dizziness, fainting, syncope, memory, and concentration troubles. A primary sudomotor involvement was recently demonstrated in hEDS with a significant reduction of sweat volume production; a finding that can explain dry skin and mucosa.
output: It could be. Problems with the autonomic nervous system (dysautonomia)—the part that automatically controls heart rate and blood pressure—are common in hEDS. The most frequent pattern is postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), where the heart races when you stand up. This can explain dizziness, palpitations, a fast heartbeat, unusual chest pain, fainting or near-fainting, tiredness, and trouble with memory and concentration ('brain fog'). The main cause seems to be a problem with the nerves that control blood vessels, though loose connective tissue in vessel walls and some medications may contribute. Some people with hEDS also sweat less, which can explain dry skin and mouth. Please discuss these symptoms with your doctor, who can assess you properly; fainting in particular should always be checked by a specialist.

instruction: A patient asks: 'I was diagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome, but I also have very flexible joints. Could it be hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Fatigue may be a principal presenting symptom in hEDS. However a clinician may diagnose CFS without appreciating the presence or pre-existence of features that may have led to a diagnosis of hEDS. The risk then is attention may be taken away from specific triggering factors for fatigue and adaptations to management specific to hEDS such as physical therapies. hEDS is likely to be substantially under-diagnosed and it is likely that some patients diagnosed with CFS may meet or would previously have met the criteria for diagnosis of hEDS. It is the authors' opinion that the literature and diagnostic methods for CFS and hEDS are of insufficient strength to reliably differentiate between these conditions in a given individual. We would conclude that in the context of hEDS one would simply use the term chronic fatigue.
output: It's possible. Fatigue can be the main symptom that brings someone with hEDS to the doctor, and a clinician may diagnose chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) without noticing the signs of hEDS. The authors believe hEDS is substantially under-diagnosed and that some people with a CFS diagnosis would meet the criteria for hEDS. Getting this right matters, because hEDS has specific fatigue triggers and needs adapted treatment, such as specialized physiotherapy. It's worth asking your doctor to assess you for hypermobility and the hEDS criteria.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. An obstetrician asks: 'What outcomes have been observed in pregnancies of women with hEDS?' Answer based on the study.
input: In a comprehensive study, Castori et al. collected gynecological and obstetric features in 82 women with hEDS. Fertility was overall preserved, as were rates of pregnancy and spontaneous abortion that were comparable with those in the Caucasian population. EDS-related symptom evolution during pregnancy seemed unpredictable as 40% of patients reported worsening symptoms (especially gastrointestinal complaints, asthenia, and pain), 13% of patients improved, and the symptoms were unchanged in the remaining 47%. Preterm delivery due to premature rupture of the membrane was reported in 10% pregnancies, which is not different from the general population. Rapid labor occurred in more than 1/3 of the cases.
output:
In 82 women with hEDS (93 pregnancies):
- Fertility, miscarriage rate, and age at menarche and menopause were comparable to the general population.
- Symptoms were unpredictable: 40% worsened (especially GI symptoms, fatigue and pain), 13% improved and 47% were unchanged.
- Preterm delivery after premature rupture of membranes occurred in 10%, which was not different from the general population.
- Rapid labor occurred in more than one-third of cases.

Plan for the possibility of rapid labor.

instruction: You are a medical educator explaining chronic pain research. Based on the abstract, what was the primary objective of studying patients with the hypermobility type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS-HT)?
input: Purpose: The Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS) is one the most prevalent heritable connective tissue disorders... Therefore, the primary objective of the study was to investigate whether pressure pain thresholds (PPTs) at both symptomatic and asymptomatic body areas differ in EDS-HT patients compared to healthy subjects. In addition, we examined the type of chronic pain EDS-HT patients experience.
output: The primary objective of the study was to investigate whether pressure pain thresholds—measured at both painful (symptomatic) and pain-free (asymptomatic) body areas—differ in patients with the hypermobility type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS-HT) compared to healthy individuals. Additionally, researchers aimed to examine the specific nature and types of chronic pain experienced by these patients.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A general surgeon asks: 'What structural GI complications occur more often in hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Morphological findings with a presumed higher rate in hEDS compared to the general population may include abdominal hernias, rectal prolapse, ptosis of internal organs, diaphragmatic hernias, and intestinal intussusceptions. Systematic data are available for abdominal hernias and rectal prolapse only, while all other features are described in single reports only. Abdominal hernias occur in up to one-fifth of the patients; the chance of occurrence increases with age, and their surgical treatment seems effective under standard procedures. Rectal prolapse is observed in more than one tenth of women. It can occur in nulliparous women but its rate is highest in those who underwent episiotomy.
output:
Structural complications with a presumed higher rate in hEDS include:
- Abdominal hernias, in up to one-fifth of patients, increasing with age. Standard surgical repair appears effective.
- Rectal prolapse, in more than one-tenth of women. It can occur in nulliparous women but is most frequent after episiotomy.

Visceroptosis, diaphragmatic hernia and intussusception have been reported only in single cases. Systematic data exist only for abdominal hernias and rectal prolapse.

instruction: A patient asks: 'When does pain usually start in hEDS, and why is it so complicated?' Answer as a health educator based on the study.
input: Pain had appeared at 10 ± 5 years old and became chronic at 20 ± 9 years old. hEDS was diagnosed at only 24 ± 10 years old. Ninety-seven percent of them had severe chronic pain, which gradually increased over time in 75% of them. The main location of pain was in joints and predominated in lower limbs. Pains in hEDS are nociceptive, neuropathic, or more frequently mixed. Diffuse hyperalgesia is not rare. Due to the phenotypical variability, an individual pain management seems necessary.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What is the typical time course of pain in hEDS, and what does it imply for diagnosis?' Answer based on the study.
input: Pain had appeared at 10 ± 5 years old and became chronic at 20 ± 9 years old. hEDS was diagnosed at only 24 ± 10 years old. Ninety-seven percent of them had severe chronic pain, which gradually increased over time in 75% of them. The main location of pain was in joints and predominated in lower limbs. Pains in hEDS are nociceptive, neuropathic, or more frequently mixed. Diffuse hyperalgesia is not rare. Due to the phenotypical variability, an individual pain management seems necessary.
output:
In 37 patients diagnosed with the 2017 criteria:
- Pain began at about 10 ± 5 years and became chronic at about 20 ± 9 years.
- hEDS was diagnosed only at about 24 ± 10 years.
- 97% had severe chronic pain, which increased over time in 75%.
- Pain was mainly articular and predominantly in the lower limbs.
- Pain was nociceptive, neuropathic or, more often, mixed, and diffuse hyperalgesia was not rare.

The decade-plus gap between pain onset and diagnosis is an opportunity for earlier recognition in pediatric and adolescent care. Phenotypic variability means pain management should be individualized.

instruction: You are a health educator. Based on the study, how long does it usually take to get diagnosed with hEDS, and how many clinicians do patients see?
input: Pain and fatigue were the primary reasons that participants began to seek medical care. In pursuit of a diagnosis, respondents saw an average of 15.6 clinicians (24% reported that they saw 20 or more), and the average time to diagnosis was 10.39 years. The majority (57%) received their official diagnosis of hEDS from a genetics specialist, followed by a rheumatologist (20%) or their primary care physician (5%). Since being diagnosed with hEDS, the average number of clinicians each participant sees has dropped to 7.48, a decrease of 52%.
output: Getting diagnosed often takes a long time. In this survey of 505 people with confirmed hEDS, pain and fatigue were the main reasons they first sought medical help. On average it took about 10.4 years to get the diagnosis, and people saw about 15.6 different clinicians along the way—a quarter saw 20 or more. Most were finally diagnosed by a geneticist (57%), followed by a rheumatologist (20%) or their family doctor (5%). There's good news too: after diagnosis, the number of clinicians people regularly saw dropped by about half, to around 7.5, showing how much a correct diagnosis can simplify care.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What does the diagnostic odyssey look like for patients with hEDS, and who usually makes the diagnosis?' Answer based on the study.
input: Pain and fatigue were the primary reasons that participants began to seek medical care. In pursuit of a diagnosis, respondents saw an average of 15.6 clinicians (24% reported that they saw 20 or more), and the average time to diagnosis was 10.39 years. The majority (57%) received their official diagnosis of hEDS from a genetics specialist, followed by a rheumatologist (20%) or their primary care physician (5%). Since being diagnosed with hEDS, the average number of clinicians each participant sees has dropped to 7.48, a decrease of 52%.
output:
In a survey of 505 patients with confirmed hEDS:
- Pain and fatigue were the main reasons patients first sought care.
- Patients saw a mean of 15.6 clinicians, and 24% saw 20 or more.
- Mean time to diagnosis was 10.39 years.
- The diagnosis was made by a geneticist in 57%, a rheumatologist in 20% and a primary care physician in 5%.
- After diagnosis, the number of clinicians seen regularly fell by 52%, to 7.48.

Earlier recognition in primary care could reduce the burden on both patients and health systems.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Are there sex differences in how joint hypermobility presents in young adults?' Answer based on the study.
input: Generalized joint hypermobility and hypermobile EDS were significantly higher in females (Table 2). The most common classes are localized asymptomatic joint hypermobility in women and localized hypermobility spectrum disorders in men (Table 1). The prevalence of skin striae was significantly higher in females, while soft tissue problems and Marfanoid habitus was significantly higher among male participants (p<0.05) (Table 3).
output:
Yes.
- Women: generalized joint hypermobility and hEDS were significantly more common, and localized asymptomatic hypermobility was the most frequent class. Skin striae were also more common.
- Men: localized hypermobility spectrum disorder was the most frequent class, and soft tissue problems (such as tendinitis or bursitis) and a marfanoid habitus were more common.

In practice, the generalized and syndromic picture is more often seen in women. In men, symptomatic localized hypermobility with soft tissue complaints may be the more typical presentation and is worth recognizing.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A university health clinician asks: 'How common is joint hypermobility in young adults, and what does that mean for my practice?' Answer based on the study.
input: In total, 77.3% (n=259) of participants had any class of joint hypermobility and 25.9% (n=87) of them had generalized class. The most common classes are localized asymptomatic joint hypermobility in women and localized hypermobility spectrum disorders in men.
output:
Joint hypermobility is very common in young adults. In this study of 335 university students aged 18–25, 77.3% had some class of joint hypermobility and 25.9% had generalized hypermobility. The most frequent classes were localized asymptomatic hypermobility in women and localized hypermobility spectrum disorder in men.

Two practical consequences:
- Hypermobility on its own is a frequent finding, not a diagnosis. Classify it as generalized, peripheral or localized, and as asymptomatic or symptomatic.
- Because it is so common, symptomatic cases are easily overlooked. Ask about pain, instability and dislocations in hypermobile young adults so that HSD or hEDS can be recognized and managed early.

instruction: A patient asks: 'What is mast cell activation syndrome and is it linked to hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) refers to an increased number of mast cells, increased mast cell mediators (e.g., histamine, tryptase, etc.), or both. The clinical symptoms of MCAS include flushing, pruritis, hypotension, asthma, diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and cramping. It remains unclear if MCAS is more common in hEDS or perhaps represents a phenocopy of hEDS. Those with EDS report a higher incidence of food sensitivities suggestive of histamine reaction. Regardless of any possible association, the presence of MCAS in hEDS might complicate the known symptoms of POTS, chronic fatigue, and gastrointestinal manifestations.
output: Mast cells are immune cells that release substances such as histamine. In mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), there are too many mast cells or they release too much of these substances, which can cause flushing, itching, low blood pressure, asthma-like symptoms, diarrhea, bloating and cramps. People with EDS more often report food sensitivities that look like histamine reactions. However, it is still not clear whether MCAS is truly more common in hEDS or just causes a similar picture. What is clear is that when someone has both, MCAS can make POTS, fatigue and digestive symptoms harder to manage.

instruction: A patient with hEDS who gets breathless with exercise asks: 'Can breathing exercises help me?' Answer based on the systematic review.
input: Even if many patients with hEDS have exertional dyspnea and breathing difficulties, the lung function cannot be considered as the cause. A benefit of the inspiratory muscle training was observed on functional exercise capacity.
output: They might. Many people with hEDS feel short of breath during exertion, yet their lung function tests are usually normal, so the lungs themselves are not thought to be the cause. In the studies reviewed, inspiratory muscle training improved how much exercise people could do. This training strengthens the muscles you use to breathe in. Ask a physiotherapist whether it's suitable for you. If breathlessness is new, sudden or severe, see a doctor first.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A pain clinician asks: 'Which validated questionnaires can I use to assess pain cognitions, fatigue, disability and general health in patients with hEDS?' Answer based on the study methods.
input: Methods: ...they completed several questionnaires assessing pain cognitions (Pain Catastrophizing Scale, Pain Vigilance and Awareness Questionnaire, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), fatigue (Checklist Individual Strength subscale fatigue), disability (Health Assessment Questionnaire), and general health status (Short Form Health Survey-36), in order to take the possible influence of these factors on PPTs into account.
output:
This study used:
- Pain cognitions: the Pain Catastrophizing Scale and the Pain Vigilance and Awareness Questionnaire.
- Anxiety and depression: the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale.
- Fatigue: the Checklist Individual Strength, fatigue subscale.
- Disability: the Health Assessment Questionnaire.
- General health: the Short Form Health Survey-36 (SF-36).

The researchers used these to account for psychological and functional factors that could influence pain measurements. In clinical practice, the same tools can help capture the biopsychosocial dimensions of pain in hEDS and track change over time.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Is there any blood biomarker or genetic test for hEDS I can order yet?' Answer based on the latest research articles.
input: Source 1 (Ritelli et al., 2024): We investigated fibronectin (FN), type I collagen (COLLI), and tenascin (TN) fragments in patient plasma using Western blotting across diverse cohorts, including patients with hEDS, HSD, classical EDS, vascular EDS, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis, and healthy donors. hEDS (94/94) and HSD (80/80) displayed a shared FN 52 kDa and COLLI 45 kDa fragment signature, absent in 150 healthy donors; classical EDS (n=10) showed no fragments, vascular EDS (n=12) only a COLLI 60 kDa fragment, and osteoarthritis, psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis displayed distinct fragment patterns. This supports their classification as a single disorder and prompting reconsideration of the hEDS criteria. Our results hold the promise for the first blood test for diagnosing hEDS/HSD. Source 2 (Forghani et al., 2025): The clinical validation and accessibility of this exploratory discovery are still in the early stages. Until then, hEDS continues to be a diagnosis of exclusion. Source 3 (Griggs et al., 2025): Proteomic analysis of serum from female hEDS patients (n=29) and matched controls revealed 35 differentially expressed proteins, 43% involved in the complement cascade; ELISA validation showed significant reductions in C1QA, C3, C8A, C8B, and C9. Source 4 (Gensemer et al., 2025): Whole-exome sequencing of 200 patients with hEDS revealed rare and low frequency variants in 14 of 15 kallikrein (KLK) genes, including a recurrent KLK15 missense variant (p.Gly226Asp) segregating in multiple families; a knock-in mouse model recapitulated hEDS features in tendons and cardiac valves.
output:
Not yet in routine practice. hEDS remains a clinical diagnosis of exclusion, but several promising research findings have emerged:

- Plasma ECM fragments (Ritelli et al., 2024): a shared fibronectin 52 kDa and type I collagen 45 kDa fragment pattern was found in all 94 hEDS and 80 HSD plasma samples and in none of 150 healthy donors, with different patterns in classical and vascular EDS, RA, PsA and OA. This could become the first blood test, and it supports viewing hEDS and HSD as one disorder. It still needs independent validation.
- Serum proteomics (Griggs et al., 2025): 35 proteins differed in 29 women with hEDS versus controls, many in the complement cascade. C1QA, C3, C8A, C8B and C9 were reduced, pointing to innate immune dysregulation.
- Genetics (Gensemer et al., 2025): exome sequencing of 200 patients found variants across kallikrein genes and a recurrent KLK15 variant (p.Gly226Asp) segregating in several families. A mouse model reproduced tendon and heart-valve features.

None of these is a validated clinical test today. Genetic testing is currently used to exclude alternative diagnoses rather than to confirm hEDS.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What is the relationship between MCAS and hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) refers to an increased number of mast cells, increased mast cell mediators (e.g., histamine, tryptase, etc.), or both. The clinical symptoms of MCAS include flushing, pruritis, hypotension, asthma, diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and cramping. It remains unclear if MCAS is more common in hEDS or perhaps represents a phenocopy of hEDS. Those with EDS report a higher incidence of food sensitivities suggestive of histamine reaction. Regardless of any possible association, the presence of MCAS in hEDS might complicate the known symptoms of POTS, chronic fatigue, and gastrointestinal manifestations.
output:
MCAS involves increased mast cells and/or mediators such as histamine and tryptase. It causes flushing, pruritus, hypotension, asthma and GI symptoms such as diarrhea, bloating and cramping.

It is unclear whether MCAS is truly more common in hEDS or represents a phenocopy with similar laxity and multisystem features. Patients with EDS do report more food sensitivities that suggest histamine reactions.

When present, MCAS can complicate POTS, fatigue and GI symptoms, so assess for it when episodic multisystem symptoms occur.

instruction: A patient asks: 'Lots of people are flexible. Why do some develop chronic pain and others don't?' Answer based on the article.
input: GJH is a prevalent clinical characteristic that is present in 2%-57% of the healthy population and is dependent on age, sex, and ethnicity. Not all individuals with GJH develop chronic complaints. It has been estimated that among individuals with GJH, approximately 3.3% of women and 0.6% of men will develop chronic complaints in terms of HMS/EDS-HT. For some, the nature of complaints is temporary and for others, GJH is even a predisposition for high-level athletic performance (eg, dance, martial arts, and gymnastics). These individuals succeed in keeping the condition manageable and may even excel in human performance. The reasons why individuals with GJH develop complaints remain elusive and are highly debated.
output: You're right that flexibility is common: generalized joint hypermobility is found in anywhere from 2% to 57% of healthy people, depending on age, sex and ethnicity. Most of them never develop long-term problems—it has been estimated that only about 3.3% of hypermobile women and 0.6% of hypermobile men go on to develop chronic complaints such as hypermobility syndrome or hEDS. For some people symptoms are only temporary, and for others flexibility is even an advantage in activities like dance, martial arts or gymnastics. Why some people develop chronic pain and others don't is still not understood and is actively debated by researchers.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Could some of my patients with a CFS/ME diagnosis actually have hEDS?' Answer based on the article.
input: Fatigue may be a principal presenting symptom in hEDS. However a clinician may diagnose CFS without appreciating the presence or pre-existence of features that may have led to a diagnosis of hEDS. The risk then is attention may be taken away from specific triggering factors for fatigue and adaptations to management specific to hEDS such as physical therapies. hEDS is likely to be substantially under-diagnosed and it is likely that some patients diagnosed with CFS may meet or would previously have met the criteria for diagnosis of hEDS. It is the authors' opinion that the literature and diagnostic methods for CFS and hEDS are of insufficient strength to reliably differentiate between these conditions in a given individual. We would conclude that in the context of hEDS one would simply use the term chronic fatigue.
output:
Possibly. Fatigue may be the presenting symptom of hEDS, and CFS is sometimes diagnosed without recognizing pre-existing hEDS features. The International Consortium committee believes hEDS is substantially under-diagnosed and that some patients with CFS meet, or previously met, hEDS criteria.

The distinction matters because hEDS-specific triggers and adaptations, such as tailored physical therapy, may otherwise be missed. In patients with CFS, examine for generalized hypermobility and screen for the other hEDS criteria. The authors recommend using the term 'chronic fatigue' in the context of hEDS.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Which autonomic manifestations are typical of hEDS, and what mechanisms are proposed?' Answer based on the article.
input: POTS, NMH, and orthostatic intolerance are common manifestations in hEDS. A study focused on hEDS highlighted POTS as the most prevalent autonomic profile in hEDS and identified sympathetic neurogenic dysfunction as the most likely explanation for dysautonomia in this condition, although connective tissue laxity and vasoactive medication may also play a role. Cardiovascular dysautonomia can easily explain orthostatic intolerance, palpitations, tachycardia, and atypical chest pain, as well as a series of neurological secondary manifestations, including fatigue, dizziness, fainting, syncope, memory, and concentration troubles. A primary sudomotor involvement was recently demonstrated in hEDS with a significant reduction of sweat volume production; a finding that can explain dry skin and mucosa.

instruction: A patient asks: 'I read that scientists may have found a blood test or a gene for hEDS. Is that true?' Answer as a health educator based on the research.
input: Source 1: In patient plasma, hEDS and HSD displayed a shared fibronectin and type I collagen fragment signature not seen in healthy donors. Our results hold the promise for the first blood test for diagnosing hEDS/HSD. Source 2: The clinical validation and accessibility of this exploratory discovery are still in the early stages. Until then, hEDS continues to be a diagnosis of exclusion. Source 3: Whole-exome sequencing of 200 patients with hEDS revealed rare variants in kallikrein (KLK) genes, including a recurrent KLK15 variant segregating in multiple families. These findings identify KLK15 as a contributor to hEDS. Source 4: Proteomic analysis revealed reduced complement proteins in hEDS, indicating systemic immune dysregulation; these findings challenge the traditional view of hEDS as solely a connective tissue disorder.
output:
There is real and encouraging progress, but nothing you can order from your doctor yet.

- An Italian team found that people with hEDS and HSD share a specific pattern of broken-down connective tissue proteins in their blood, a pattern not seen in healthy people. This could one day become the first blood test, but it still needs to be confirmed by other researchers.
- A US team found changes in genes called kallikreins, including one specific variant in the KLK15 gene that runs in several families with hEDS. It is likely one contributor rather than the cause for everyone.
- Another study found differences in immune system proteins (the complement system), suggesting hEDS involves the immune system as well as connective tissue.

For now, hEDS is still diagnosed through a clinical examination, but these studies may lead to objective tests and new treatments in the future.

instruction: You are a medical educator. Based on the article, what is the 5-point questionnaire and how is it used in diagnosing hEDS?
input: For conditions that affect the Beighton score, such as previous surgeries and amputation of the joint, a self-reported five-point questionnaire (5PQ) is used to consider historic hypermobility. 1. Can you now (or could you ever) place your hands flat on the floor without bending your knees? 2. Can you now (or could you ever) bend your thumb to touch your forearm? 3. As a child did you amuse your friends by contorting your body into strange shapes or could you do the splits? 4. As a child or teenager did your shoulder or kneecap dislocate on more than one occasion? 5. Do you consider yourself double-jointed? To take the historic JH into account, the committee decided to add one point to the Beighton score, when it is one point below the cut-off point and if two or more items in the 5PQ are positive.
output: The 5-point questionnaire is a short set of yes/no questions about your flexibility now and in the past. It asks whether you can (or ever could) put your hands flat on the floor with straight knees; whether you can (or ever could) bend your thumb to touch your forearm; whether as a child you entertained friends by contorting your body or doing the splits; whether as a child or teenager your shoulder or kneecap dislocated more than once; and whether you consider yourself double-jointed. It is useful because flexibility decreases with age, surgery or injury. If your Beighton score is just one point below the cut-off and you answer 'yes' to two or more questions, one point is added to your score.

instruction: You are a medical educator explaining research methodology. Based on the abstract, what questionnaires were used to evaluate potential confounding factors like psychological state and fatigue in EDS-HT patients?
input: Methods: ...they completed several questionnaires assessing pain cognitions (Pain Catastrophizing Scale, Pain Vigilance and Awareness Questionnaire, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), fatigue (Checklist Individual Strength subscale fatigue), disability (Health Assessment Questionnaire), and general health status (Short Form Health Survey-36), in order to take the possible influence of these factors on PPTs into account.
output: To ensure that psychological factors, fatigue, or general disability didn't skew the pain threshold results, researchers had participants complete several standardized tools, including the Pain Catastrophizing Scale, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, a fatigue checklist, a health assessment questionnaire, and the Short Form Health Survey-36.

instruction: You are a medical educator explaining research results. Based on the study, how did pressure pain thresholds (PPTs) in EDS-HT patients compare to healthy controls?
input: Results: The EDS-HT patient group demonstrated significantly lower PPTs compared to the control group for all zones. The mean (SD) PPT was 2.9 (1.62) kg/cm2 in the EDS-HT patients and 5.2 (1.88) kg/cm2 in the controls (P<0.001). Also at asymptomatic (pain-free) zones, EDS-HT patients systematically showed significantly lower pain thresholds compared to the healthy subjects.
output: The study found that patients with EDS-HT had significantly lower pressure pain thresholds (PPTs) across all tested body zones compared to healthy controls (with a mean of 2.9 kg/cm2 versus 5.2 kg/cm2, P<0.001). Crucially, even in pain-free (asymptomatic) areas of the body, EDS-HT patients systematically showed lower pain thresholds, providing evidence of generalized secondary hyperalgesia and a sensitized central nervous system.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'How do I use the five-point questionnaire (5PQ) when assessing hypermobility?' Answer based on the article.
input: For conditions that affect the Beighton score, such as previous surgeries and amputation of the joint, a self-reported five-point questionnaire (5PQ) is used to consider historic hypermobility. 1. Can you now (or could you ever) place your hands flat on the floor without bending your knees? 2. Can you now (or could you ever) bend your thumb to touch your forearm? 3. As a child did you amuse your friends by contorting your body into strange shapes or could you do the splits? 4. As a child or teenager did your shoulder or kneecap dislocate on more than one occasion? 5. Do you consider yourself double-jointed? To take the historic JH into account, the committee decided to add one point to the Beighton score, when it is one point below the cut-off point and if two or more items in the 5PQ are positive.
output:
The 5PQ captures historical hypermobility when the current Beighton score may underestimate it because of age, surgery, injury or amputation. It asks:
1. Can you now, or could you ever, place your hands flat on the floor without bending your knees?
2. Can you now, or could you ever, bend your thumb to touch your forearm?
3. As a child, did you contort your body or do the splits?
4. As a child or teenager, did your shoulder or kneecap dislocate more than once?
5. Do you consider yourself double-jointed?

Under the 2017 criteria, if the Beighton score is one point below the age-specific cut-off and two or more 5PQ answers are positive, add one point to the score.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'Many patients with hEDS report exertional dyspnea with normal lung function. Is there an intervention with evidence?' Answer based on the review.
input: Even if many patients with hEDS have exertional dyspnea and breathing difficulties, the lung function cannot be considered as the cause. A benefit of the inspiratory muscle training was observed on functional exercise capacity.
output:
Exertional dyspnea and breathing difficulties are common in hEDS, but lung function cannot be considered the cause.

In the systematic review, inspiratory muscle training improved functional exercise capacity. Consider a physiotherapy referral for inspiratory muscle training once other causes of dyspnea have been appropriately assessed.

instruction: A pregnant woman with hEDS asks: 'Will my symptoms get worse during pregnancy?' Answer based on the article.
input: In a comprehensive study, Castori et al. collected gynecological and obstetric features in 82 women with hEDS. Fertility was overall preserved, as were rates of pregnancy and spontaneous abortion that were comparable with those in the Caucasian population. EDS-related symptom evolution during pregnancy seemed unpredictable as 40% of patients reported worsening symptoms (especially gastrointestinal complaints, asthenia, and pain), 13% of patients improved, and the symptoms were unchanged in the remaining 47%. Preterm delivery due to premature rupture of the membrane was reported in 10% pregnancies, which is not different from the general population. Rapid labor occurred in more than 1/3 of the cases.
output: It's hard to predict. In a study of 82 women with hEDS, about 40% felt worse during pregnancy (especially digestive problems, tiredness and pain), 13% actually felt better, and 47% noticed no change. Reassuringly, fertility and miscarriage rates were similar to the general population, and early delivery after the waters broke early (10% of pregnancies) was not more common than usual. One thing to know: labor was fast in more than a third of cases, so it is worth discussing a birth plan with your obstetric team early.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What do studies show about bone mineral density in joint hypermobility?' Answer based on the article.
input: Reduced BMD by ultrasound and lower excretion of urinary hydroxylysylpyridinoline cross-links and lysylpyridinoline cross-links were demonstrated in 15 children with 'symptomatic' GJH compared to 95 healthy prepubertal children. By contrast, another study suggests that a high Beighton score may be a marker of fitness, reduced rate of knee osteoarthritis and increased (rather than reduced) hip BMD in postmenopausal women. A third study showed reduced BMD (mild osteopenia) in 23 premenopausal hypermobile women compared to controls by DXA at some sites but not others. As expected from the early literature and the nosologic confusion among EDS, GJH, and JHS, the published data may be hard to apply to 'pure' hEDS. It is unclear if hEDS is associated with osteoporosis in adults, especially premenopausal women.
output:
The results are inconsistent:
- 15 children with symptomatic generalized hypermobility had reduced ultrasound BMD and lower urinary collagen cross-link excretion than 95 healthy prepubertal children.
- In postmenopausal women, a high Beighton score was associated with higher hip BMD, less knee OA and greater fitness.
- 23 premenopausal hypermobile women had mild osteopenia on DXA at some sites but not others.

Because of earlier diagnostic confusion between EDS, GJH and JHS, these data are hard to apply to hEDS itself. Whether hEDS causes osteoporosis in adults remains unclear. Assess bone health on standard clinical grounds rather than assuming the diagnosis implies low BMD.

instruction: You are a clinical decision-support assistant for physicians and other clinicians who do not specialize in hypermobility disorders. A clinician asks: 'What proportion of people with generalized joint hypermobility become symptomatic?' Answer based on the article.
input: GJH is a prevalent clinical characteristic that is present in 2%-57% of the healthy population and is dependent on age, sex, and ethnicity. Not all individuals with GJH develop chronic complaints. It has been estimated that among individuals with GJH, approximately 3.3% of women and 0.6% of men will develop chronic complaints in terms of HMS/EDS-HT. For some, the nature of complaints is temporary and for others, GJH is even a predisposition for high-level athletic performance (eg, dance, martial arts, and gymnastics). These individuals succeed in keeping the condition manageable and may even excel in human performance. The reasons why individuals with GJH develop complaints remain elusive and are highly debated.
output:
Generalized joint hypermobility is present in 2–57% of the healthy population, depending on age, sex and ethnicity. Only a minority develop chronic complaints: an estimated 3.3% of hypermobile women and 0.6% of hypermobile men develop HMS/EDS-HT. In some people, complaints are temporary. Others, such as dancers, martial artists and gymnasts, may even benefit from their hypermobility.

It is unclear why some people become symptomatic, and clinician unawareness probably leads to underestimation. A positive Beighton score alone should not be over-interpreted, but symptomatic patients deserve evaluation.

instruction: You are a health educator answering a user's question. Based on the article, explain if joint hypermobility is common among young adults.
input: In total, 77.3% (n=259) of participants had any class of joint hypermobility and 25.9% (n=87) of them had generalized class. The most common classes are localized asymptomatic joint hypermobility in women and localized hypermobility spectrum disorders in men.
output: Yes, joint hypermobility is actually surprisingly common among young adults. A study of university students aged 18 to 25 found that over 77% of participants had some form of joint hypermobility (ranging from localized forms in specific joints to generalized hypermobility). Interestingly, localized forms were most common—specifically in single joints or body parts, appearing as localized asymptomatic hypermobility in women and localized spectrum disorders in men.
